usage: Two servings of pork belly, please
Meat is ordered by 인분 (serving), never by piece — this is the core ordering phrase.
Pork belly with a shot of soju
에 here marks the food you pair a drink with; the most iconic Korean food-and-drink combo.
We grill and eat pork belly
굽다 → 구워 (ㅂ-irregular); you cook it yourself at the table-top grill.
The fat renders right out, which is great
쫙 빠지다 is the set phrase Koreans use to praise well-grilled 삼겹살.
examples: 삼겹살 먹으러 갈래요?
Want to go eat pork belly?
The everyday casual invite; 먹으러 가다 = go in order to eat.
삼겹살 다 익었어요?
Is the pork belly fully cooked?
익다 = (food) to be cooked through; ask before you pick a piece off the grill.
삼겹살은 쌈에 싸서 먹어야 제맛이에요.
Pork belly only tastes right wrapped in a lettuce leaf.
쌈 = the lettuce/perilla wrap; -아야 제맛이다 = 'it's only truly good when…', a very natural food cliché.
nuance: 삼겹살 literally breaks down as 삼(三, three) + 겹(layer) + 살(flesh) — 'three-layered meat' — naming the alternating stripes of fat and lean in pork belly, and it is the single most iconic Korean BBQ cut and a default casual group meal. Don't confuse it with 목살 (pork neck/collar, leaner) or 오겹살 (a five-layer belly cut with the skin on); waiters list these as separate menu lines. Register-wise the word itself is neutral, but the situation is firmly casual — friends, 회식 work dinners, late nights with soju — never a formal banquet. The pitfall for English speakers is the counter: 'a piece of pork belly' tempts you into 삼겹살 한 개, but you must order by 인분 (삼겹살 2인분), and you say 구워 먹다 (grill-and-eat) rather than the English 'have a barbecue,' because here you do the grilling yourself.

mistakes: Saying 삼겹살 한 개 — meat is counted by 인분 (serving), so the correct order is 삼겹살 1인분 / 2인분.
Calling any grilled pork 삼겹살 — 삼겹살 is specifically the belly cut; 목살 (neck) and 항정살 (jowl) are different lines on the menu.
Using 만들다 ('make') for grilling at the table — Koreans say 삼겹살 구워 먹다 (grill and eat), not 삼겹살 만들다.

usage: 갈비 alone is ambiguous, so the species prefix 돼지/소 is almost always attached.
양념 = seasoning/marinade; -로 주세요 picks one option among several.
Grilled 갈비 is counted by 인분; ~이요 is the quick spoken order form.
One bowl of rib soup, please
갈비탕 is a soup dish counted by 그릇 (bowl), not 인분 — a different format from grilled 갈비.
examples: 여기는 양념갈비가 유명해요.
This place is famous for its marinated ribs.
은/는 here flags 양념갈비 as the topic/specialty being contrasted.
갈비는 좀 비싸지만 가끔 먹을 만해요.
Ribs are a bit pricey, but worth it once in a while.
-(으)ㄹ 만하다 = 'worth doing'; beef 갈비 especially reads as a splurge.
점심에 갈비탕 먹으러 갈까요?
Shall we go for rib soup at lunch?
-(으)ㄹ까요? softly proposes a plan; 갈비탕 is a comforting everyday lunch.
nuance: 갈비 means the rib cut, and it heads a whole family of dishes: grilled plain 생갈비, sweet-marinated 양념갈비, the braised 갈비찜, and the soup 갈비탕. The crucial ambiguity for a learner is species — 갈비 can be beef or pork, so Koreans say 소갈비 or 돼지갈비 to be clear, and at many casual BBQ joints an unqualified '갈비' defaults to the cheaper 돼지갈비, while 소갈비 reads as a costly, special-occasion meal. Note the cut sits next to 삼겹살 and 등심 as a grilling option but, unlike them, has a famous sweet marinade tradition (soy, sugar, pear, garlic). The English-speaker trap is treating 갈비 as automatically 'beef ribs' and then conflating the grilled cut with the soup: 갈비 is the rib itself, whereas 갈비탕 (-탕 = clear soup) is a boiled dish — ordering one expecting the other is a common mix-up.

Counting 갈비탕 by 인분 — soups are counted by 그릇 (bowl): 갈비탕 한 그릇, while grilled 갈비 uses 인분.

usage: A leaner premium beef cut at 소고기 (beef) restaurants, counted by 인분.
부드럽다 (ㅂ-irregular → 부드러워요) is the key praise word for a good cut.
Between sirloin and tenderloin, which is better?
N하고 N 중에 = 'among A and B'; the two cuts are constantly compared.
I'll have the ribeye (marbled sirloin), please
꽃등심 = the marbled 'flower' upgrade of 등심, a prized higher-grade cut.
examples: 소고깃집에서는 등심이 기본이에요.
At a beef restaurant, sirloin is the standard order.
기본 = the default/basic choice; -에서는 sets the location as the frame.
꽃등심은 마블링이 좋아서 더 비싸요.
Ribeye has good marbling, so it costs more.
-아서 links cause→result; 마블링 (marbling) is the price driver for beef.
등심은 너무 익히면 질겨져요.
If you overcook sirloin, it turns tough.
익히다 = to cook (transitive); 질겨지다 = to become chewy/tough — lean cuts dry out.
nuance: 등심 is the loin/sirloin, the workhorse grilling cut at beef-focused restaurants — relatively lean yet tender, and the cut people mean by default when they say 'let's get 소고기.' It is a native Korean compound, 등 (back) + 심 (the core/inner flesh), not a Sino-Korean word, so don't go looking for a 한자 reading. The synonym boundary to nail is 등심 vs 안심: both are premium, but 등심 (sirloin, from the back) has a touch more fat and bite, while 안심 (tenderloin) is leaner and softer; menus list them side by side, and the marbled upgrade 꽃등심 ('flower sirloin' = ribeye) is the splurge tier above plain 등심. Collocations cluster around texture and grade: 등심이 부드럽다 (tender), 마블링이 좋다 (well-marbled), 질겨지다 (gets tough). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'sirloin/loin' loosely and ordering 등심 expecting cheap pork — it is almost always higher-priced beef — and overcooking it the way you might a steak, when Koreans grill these cuts only briefly to keep them 부드럽다.

mistakes: Confusing 등심 (sirloin, slightly fattier, more bite) with 안심 (tenderloin, leaner and softer) — they are adjacent but distinct menu cuts.

Grilling 등심 long like a well-done steak — overcooking makes it 질겨지다 (tough); Koreans sear it briefly.

usage: 안심 is the leanest, most tender cut and the classic steak choice; -로 picks the option.
Tenderloin is more tender than sirloin
N보다 = 'than N'; the standard comparison that defines 안심.
Counted by 인분 at beef restaurants, like other grilling cuts.
안심 exists for pork too and is the lean cut used in 돈가스 (cutlet).
examples: 안심은 기름기가 적어서 담백해요.
Tenderloin is low in fat, so it's clean and mild.
기름기 = fattiness; 담백하다 = mild, non-greasy — the signature flavor note for lean cuts.
스테이크는 안심으로 주문했어요.
I ordered the steak as tenderloin.
-(으)로 marks the material/choice the steak is made from.
안심이라서 좀 더 비쌌어요.
Because it was tenderloin, it was a bit pricier.
N(이)라서 = 'because it is N'; 안심 is a premium lean cut.
nuance: 안심 is the tenderloin — the leanest, softest muscle (it does little work), which is why it is the go-to for 스테이크 and why people praise it as 담백하다 (mild and clean, not greasy) and 부드럽다 (tender). The key contrast is 안심 vs 등심: counter to English intuition, the 'tenderloin' 안심 is the leaner one, while 등심 (sirloin) carries a bit more fat and chew — learners often guess the opposite. The headache here is the homonym: 안심 the cut is spelled identically to the verb 안심하다 (安心하다, 'to feel relieved / at ease', literally 'settle the heart'), so 안심하세요 means 'don't worry,' not anything about meat — only context (a menu vs. a conversation) disambiguates. Collocations: 안심 스테이크, 기름기가 적다, 담백하다. The pitfall is twofold — reading the meat 안심 as the feeling-relieved word, and assuming the 'tender' cut must be the fattier one when it is actually the leanest.

usage: Give me one chicken drumstick, please
It's a discrete piece, so it's counted with 하나/개, not 인분.
살 = the flesh; 닭다리살 is the de-boned thigh/leg meat used in bowls and lunchboxes.
Drumsticks are juicier than chicken breast
촉촉하다 = moist/juicy; the standard leg-vs-breast contrast.
I go for the drumstick first
N부터 = 'starting from N'; signals the leg is your favorite piece.
examples: 치킨 시키면 저는 닭다리 먼저 먹어요.
When we order fried chicken, I eat the drumstick first.
시키다 = to order (food); 먼저 = first — the popular piece everyone reaches for.
이건 닭다리살로 만든 도시락이에요.
This is a lunchbox made with boneless chicken-leg meat.
-(으)로 만들다 = 'made with'; 닭다리살 (de-boned) is common in 도시락.
애들은 보통 닭다리를 더 좋아해요.
Kids usually like the drumsticks more.
보통 = usually; the leg is the easy-to-hold, kid-friendly piece.
nuance: 닭다리 is a transparent compound, 닭(chicken) + 다리(leg), meaning the drumstick/leg — widely considered the juiciest, most flavorful part and often the most fought-over piece when a group shares 치킨 (fried chicken). The useful derived form is 닭다리살, the boneless leg/thigh meat (살 = flesh) that fills 도시락 lunchboxes and rice bowls; contrast it with 닭가슴살 (breast meat), the leaner, drier cut that dieters and gym-goers eat. Texture words pair naturally: 닭다리는 촉촉하다 (juicy/moist) versus 닭가슴살은 퍽퍽하다 (dry/mealy). The counting pitfall matters: because 닭다리 is one bone-in piece, count it with 개/하나 (닭다리 하나), never 인분, which is for table-grilled meat by the portion. A second English-speaker trap is treating leg and breast as interchangeable 'chicken' — Koreans care about the cut, so 닭다리 vs 닭가슴살 is a real menu-and-preference distinction, not a throwaway detail.

Treating 닭다리 (leg, juicy) and 닭가슴살 (breast, lean/dry) as the same 'chicken' — they differ a lot in fat and texture.
Saying 닭다리가 말랐어요 for 'the leg is dry' — use 퍽퍽하다 for dry meat; 마르다 means a body/object is thin or dried out.

usage: N 알레르기(가) 있다 = 'have an N allergy'; a safety-critical phrase when ordering.
튀김 = deep-fried dish; one of the most common 새우 preparations.
빼다 = to remove/omit; -아 주세요 politely requests it be taken out.
Does this have shrimp in it?
들어가다 here = (an ingredient) to be included; the go-to question for allergies.
examples: 새우 좋아해요?
Do you like shrimp?
A simple everyday preference question with the bare noun.
이 볶음밥에 새우 들어가요?
Does this fried rice have shrimp in it?
들어가다 asks whether an ingredient is inside — essential for checking allergens.
새우 알레르기가 있어서 새우는 꼭 빼 주세요.
I have a shrimp allergy, so please be sure to leave the shrimp out.
Chain allergy + 꼭(definitely) + 빼 주세요 to order safely in a real situation.
nuance: 새우 (shrimp/prawn) is one of the most ubiquitous proteins in Korean cooking — fried as 새우튀김, in 볶음밥 (fried rice), in stews, in 깐쇼새우 — so the words around it are practical survival vocabulary, especially 새우 알레르기 있어요 and 새우 빼 주세요 for anyone with a shellfish allergy. Watch the verb 들어가다 ('to go in', here 'to be an ingredient'): 새우 들어가요? literally 'does shrimp go in?' is exactly how you ask whether a dish contains it. Keep 새우 distinct from neighboring shellfish — 게 (crab), 가재 (crayfish/lobster), 조개 (clam) — since 'seafood' in English blurs them but Korean menus name each. The big English-speaker pitfall is the omission phrase: learners reach for 새우 없어요 ('there's no shrimp') to mean 'I can't eat shrimp,' which only states a fact about availability; to make a request you must say 새우 빼 주세요 (remove the shrimp) or state the allergy outright.

Lumping 새우 with 게 (crab) or 가재 (crayfish) as one 'seafood' — Korean names each shellfish separately on menus.
Using 있다/없다 to ask if a dish contains shrimp — the natural verb is 들어가다: 새우 들어가요?

usage: 볶음 = stir-fry; a popular spicy dish eaten with rice.
질기다 = tough/chewy; squid turns rubbery when overcooked.
마르다 → 마른 (modifier); a classic 안주 (drinking snack) and beer companion.
Whole animals/seafood are counted with 마리, not 개.
examples: 오징어 좋아하세요?
Do you like squid?
Polite everyday preference question with -세요.
오징어볶음은 밥이랑 같이 먹으면 진짜 맛있어요.
Spicy stir-fried squid is really good eaten with rice.
N(이)랑 같이 = 'together with N'; a staple rice-pairing dish.
오징어를 너무 오래 익히면 질겨져요.
If you cook squid too long, it gets rubbery.
익히다 = to cook (transitive); 질겨지다 = to turn tough — cook squid only briefly.
nuance: 오징어 (squid) is a native everyday word that shows up across the menu: the spicy stir-fry 오징어볶음 eaten over rice, grilled 오징어구이, and especially the dried 마른 오징어, a quintessential 안주 (drinking snack) sold in every convenience store. The texture vocabulary is central — 질기다 (chewy/rubbery) and its change form 질겨지다 (to become tough) — because Koreans know squid must be cooked briefly or it turns rubbery, the opposite of beef which can simmer. The counting pitfall is real: a whole squid is 한 마리 (마리 counts animals and seafood), never 한 개. The other English-speaker trap is lumping cephalopods together: 오징어 (squid), 문어 (octopus), and 낙지 (small/long-arm octopus) are three distinct items with different dishes and prices, so calling all of them 'squid' will get you the wrong thing — for example 낙지볶음 and 오징어볶음 are separate menu lines.

Calling 문어 (octopus) or 낙지 (small octopus) '오징어' — they are different animals and different dishes on the menu.
Using 딱딱하다 (hard, like a rock) for overcooked squid — the right word is 질기다 (chewy/rubbery).

usage: 구이 = grilled dish; a popular seaside meal where you grill them at the table.
탕 = clear soup; clams give it a clean, savory broth.
Unopened clams during cooking are dead beforehand and shouldn't be eaten.
The broth is clean and refreshing
시원하다 of soup = savory and clean-tasting, NOT temperature-cold.
examples: 바닷가에서 조개구이 먹었어요.
We had grilled clams at the seaside.
-에서 marks the place of the action; 조개구이 is a classic coastal order.
이 칼국수는 조개를 많이 넣어서 국물이 시원해요.
This noodle soup has lots of clams, so the broth is clean and savory.
-아서 links cause→result; 시원하다 praises a clear, umami broth (not cold).
조개는 모래가 있을 수 있으니까 잘 씻어요.
Clams can have sand, so wash them well.
-(으)니까 gives the reason; 해감 (purging sand) is a real prep step before cooking.
nuance: 조개 is the general native word for clams and bivalve shellfish, and it heads dishes like 조개구이 (grilled clams) and 조개탕 (-탕, clear soup). Because it is a category word, when a recipe or menu needs a specific shellfish you switch to the precise name — 바지락 (manila clam), 홍합 (mussel), 가리비 (scallop), 꼬막 (cockle) — so calling all of them just 조개 can be too vague. The flavor cliché to internalize is 국물이 시원하다: with seafood broth, 시원하다 does NOT mean 'cold' but 'clean, brisk, savory' — a deeply Korean way to praise soup, and the classic English-speaker mistranslation. A second pitfall is the safety note baked into 조개가 안 열렸어요: an unopened clam after cooking should be discarded, and Koreans routinely 해감 (soak to purge sand) before cooking, so 모래 (sand) and 씻다 (wash) are common partner words.

usage: 구이 = grilled; a staple home-style and 백반 set-meal fish dish.
조림 = simmered in seasoned (often spicy) sauce, classically with radish (무).
비리다 = the specific fishy smell/taste of seafood, common with oily fish.
손 = a market counter meaning two fish sold as a set.
examples: 백반집에서 고등어구이가 자주 나와요.
Grilled mackerel often comes out at home-style set-meal places.
나오다 = (a dish) to be served/come out; 백반 meals frequently include 고등어구이.
고등어조림은 무랑 같이 조리면 맛있어요.
Braised mackerel is delicious simmered together with radish.
N(이)랑 같이 = with N; 무 (radish) is the classic 조림 partner.
고등어는 구울 때 냄새가 좀 나요.
Mackerel gives off a bit of a smell when grilling.
-(으)ㄹ 때 = 'when ~ing'; 냄새가 나다 = a smell arises — oily fish are aromatic while cooking.
nuance: 고등어 (mackerel) is an everyday, cheap, oily fish that anchors home cooking and 백반 (home-style set-meal) tables as 고등어구이 (grilled) or 고등어조림 (braised with radish). The flavor word to learn precisely is 비리다 — the particular 'fishy' smell/taste of not-fresh seafood — which is its own adjective, distinct from generic 냄새가 나다 (to give off a smell): you say 고등어가 비려요, not 고등어 냄새 나빠요, which sounds unnatural. A practical market detail is the counter 손: fish like mackerel are often sold 한 손, meaning a pair (two fish), so 고등어 한 손 ≠ one fish. Keep 고등어 distinct from other common fish on a 생선 (fish) menu — 갈치 (hairtail), 삼치 (Spanish mackerel), 꽁치 (saury) — since a recipe asking for mackerel specifically won't accept a generic 생선. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'bad smell' vocabulary when the precise, non-judgmental word 비리다 is what Koreans actually use for seafood.

usage: 초밥 = vinegared-rice sushi; 연어 is one of the most popular toppings in Korea.
덮밥 = a bowl of rice covered with toppings; an easy everyday lunch.
회 = sliced raw fish; 연어회 is hugely popular, often all-you-can-eat (무한리필).
신선하다 = fresh; the key quality word for anything served raw.
examples: 저는 회 중에서 연어를 제일 좋아해요.
Among sashimi options, I like salmon the most.
N 중에서 = 'among N'; 제일 = the most — 연어 is a top 회 pick.
연어 덮밥 하나랑 미소국 주세요.
One salmon rice bowl and a miso soup, please.
N 하나랑 N = 'one N and N'; a very common lunch order.
연어는 구워 먹어도 맛있어요.
Salmon is also delicious grilled.
-아도 = 'even if / also'; 연어 works raw or cooked as 연어구이.
nuance: 연어 (鰱魚, salmon) has surged in popularity in Korea, especially raw as 연어회 and 연어 초밥 and in 연어 덮밥 rice bowls, and it's a trendy, mild, fatty option that newcomers gravitate to before tackling more traditional fish. The contrast worth knowing is 연어 (salmon) vs 송어 (trout): they look similar and both appear raw, but they're different fish, and what budget all-you-can-eat 'salmon' spots serve is sometimes 송어 — so the names aren't interchangeable. Quality vocabulary centers on 신선하다 (fresh), essential since it's eaten raw. A cultural pitfall for English speakers: don't assume every traditional 횟집 (sashimi restaurant) features 연어 — long-established 횟집 often specialize in lean white fish like 광어 (flatfish) and 우럭 (rockfish), and 연어 is more a feature of modern, casual, or 무한리필 (all-you-can-eat) places. Also note 연어 is mild, so the 비리다 (fishy) complaint applies less to it than to oily fish like 고등어.

usage: One serving of grilled intestines, please
Ordered by 인분 at a 곱창집; one serving is fairly small and pricey.
Intestines with a shot of soju
에 pairs the food with the drink; a beloved late-night 술안주 combo.
곱창 = small intestine; 막창 (last stomach) and 대창 (large intestine) are distinct cuts.
Fried rice at the end, please
볶음밥 fried in the leftover 곱창 pan is the traditional finish to the meal.
examples: 오늘 곱창에 소주 한잔 어때요?
How about grilled intestines and soju tonight?
N 어때요? = 'how about N?'; 곱창 is a classic 술안주 (drinking food).
곱창은 호불호가 좀 갈려요.
People are pretty divided on grilled intestines.
호불호가 갈리다 = opinions split (love-it-or-hate-it); a very natural set phrase.
곱창 다 먹고 마지막에 볶음밥 꼭 먹어요.
After finishing the intestines, we always get fried rice at the end.
다 먹다 = eat it all up; the pan-fried 볶음밥 finale is a must.
nuance: 곱창 is grilled small intestine (most often beef, but 돼지곱창 / pork is common and cheaper), a beloved but polarizing 술안주 (drinking food) eaten late at night with soju, and the meal traditionally ends with 볶음밥 fried in the rich leftover-fat pan. The vocabulary Koreans attach to it is telling: it's a 호불호(가) 갈리는 음식 — a 'love-it-or-hate-it' food (호불호 好不好 = liking/disliking) — so that phrase is worth memorizing here. The crucial distinction is among offal cuts: 곱창 (small intestine, chewy with creamy filling), 대창 (large intestine, fattier, richer), and 막창 (the fourth stomach chamber, common in Daegu) are three different things with different textures and prices, not synonyms. Register is firmly casual and nighttime — you wouldn't propose 곱창 for a formal lunch. The English-speaker pitfall is treating all 'intestines/offal' as one item (and overlooking that an unqualified 곱창 may be pork), plus expecting it cheap — by weight 곱창 is often pricier than 삼겹살.

usage: 회 = sliced raw fish, eaten at a 횟집; -(으)러 가다 = go in order to do.
모둠 = assorted; a mixed platter of several fish, great when undecided.
Sashimi is counted by 접시 (plate), reflecting how it's served.
I'm not great with raw fish
잘 못 먹다 = can't really eat / am not good with — a soft, polite decline.
examples: 회 좋아하세요?
Do you like sashimi?
Polite preference question with -세요; a common ice-breaker by the coast.
모둠회 시키면 여러 종류 나와요.
If you order the assorted platter, several kinds come out.
시키다 = to order; 나오다 = to be served — 모둠회 covers indecision.
저는 익힌 게 좋아서 회는 잘 안 먹어요.
I prefer cooked food, so I don't really eat raw fish.
익힌 거 = cooked thing; a natural, non-awkward way to opt out of 회.
nuance: 회 (膾, sliced raw fish) is the centerpiece of Korean coastal dining, served at a 횟집 (sashimi restaurant) and typically shared as a 모둠회 (assorted) platter with banchan and a follow-up 매운탕 (spicy fish stew) made from the bones. The boundary that trips up English speakers is 회 vs 초밥 (sushi): 회 is JUST the sliced raw fish — no rice — whereas 초밥 is the vinegared-rice nigiri; so '연어회' is plain salmon slices while '연어 초밥' sits on rice. Korean overwhelmingly borrows Japanese 'sashimi/sushi' concepts but keeps its own words and rituals (eaten with 초장 chili-vinegar sauce or 쌈, lots of soju). Counting is by 접시 (plate), not 인분. Register: 회 먹으러 가요 is a casual, social, often celebratory or seaside-trip invitation. The other pitfall is the homonym field — 회 also lives inside 회사 (company), 회의 (meeting), 회식 (work dinner) — but standalone 회 in a food/restaurant context unambiguously means the raw fish; context, especially the word 횟집, makes it clear.
